planting.note: Set out vegetatively-propagated transplants in spring once the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow air movement through the tidy mounded foliage. EverLast Red Flash is part of the EverLast series bred for continuous rebloom without a hard mid-summer rest, so deadheading spent stems keeps new buds forming.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean to average, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil, since heavy wet ground is the main threat to this cultivar's longevity. The flowers carry a two-tone red-and-white 'flash' pattern typical of the EverLast breeding line, held above a compact, grassy blue-green mound that resists the floppy habit of older dianthus types. Shear lightly after the first flush to encourage the repeat bloom the series is bred for, and avoid mulching right up against the crown to prevent rot. Established plants tolerate heat and short dry spells better than most spring-blooming pinks.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; Rosy Robin belongs to the Feathered Friends line of bred, controlled-spread ajuga selected to carpet ground without the aggressive runners of common bugleweed.

directions: Grow in part sun to light shade with consistent moisture; full sun in hot climates can scorch the colorful foliage, while deep shade mutes the rosy pink-and-bronze leaf color the cultivar is selected for. Short spikes of blue flowers rise above the foliage mat in late spring, attracting early bees without overwhelming the leaf display that is the main ornamental draw. Unlike seed-grown species ajuga, this bred selection spreads at a slower, more predictable rate, making it easier to keep inside a border edge or between pavers. Divide congested patches every few years in spring to refresh vigor and leaf color.

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed into well-drained soil or containers; Blazen Compact Blue is bred to self-clean and stay tighter than older fan flower selections, suiting hanging baskets as well as ground-level beds.

directions: Grow in full sun with excellent drainage; fan flower is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established and declines quickly in soggy or overly rich soil. Distinctive one-sided, fan-shaped blue flowers appear continuously from late spring through fall without deadheading, since spent blooms drop cleanly on their own. In frost-free zones it behaves as a woody-based perennial, while gardeners farther north grow it as a warm-season annual that is discarded or overwintered indoors as cuttings. Pinch stem tips occasionally on young plants to encourage the dense, mounding-to-trailing habit this compact selection is bred for.

planting.note: Transplant into full sun after the last frost once nights stay reliably warm; Serafina Raspberry belongs to a compact, uniform summer snapdragon series bred for strong heat tolerance and season-long color in beds, borders, and containers.

directions: Plant in full sun and moderately fertile, well-drained soil; angelonia thrives in the heat and humidity of mid-summer when many other bedding annuals fade. Upright spikes of raspberry-pink, orchid-like flowers open continuously along the stems from early summer into fall, and the plant is naturally self-cleaning so spent flowers are not noticeable. It shrugs off both heat and short dry spells but benefits from regular watering during extended drought to keep flower production high. In zones 9-11 it can persist as a woody-based perennial, while colder climates treat it as a warm-season annual.

planting.note: Plant transplants or hanging basket starts after the last frost into well-drained soil or mix; blue pimpernel flowers best when roots are kept on the dry side between waterings.

directions: Grow in full sun with sharp drainage; this low, trailing selection opens its intense true-blue, saucer-shaped flowers most fully in bright sun and closes them on cloudy or rainy days. It is well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and front-of-border edging where its spreading habit can cascade over an edge. Overwatering and heavy soil are the most common causes of decline, so let the surface dry between waterings rather than keeping it constantly moist. In mild coastal or desert climates it can act as a short-lived perennial, while elsewhere it is best treated as a warm-season annual.

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; African daisy is bred from South African species that resent wet feet and reward neglect over pampering.

directions: Plant in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; this orange-flamed selection produces large daisy-form blooms with a dark central disc held on sturdy stems above silvery-green foliage. It tolerates heat, salt spray, and drought far better than it tolerates soggy or overly fertile soil, which quickly leads to rot and sparse flowering. Deadheading spent flower heads keeps the plant producing new buds over a longer season. Where winters stay frost-free it persists as a woody-based perennial; elsewhere it is grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors from cuttings.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperature, then transplant into full sun once nights stay reliably above 50F; Monteverde Genovese is a classic sweet-leaf Genovese type bred for uniform, vigorous growth.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container on a sunny patio, after the danger of frost has fully passed since basil is highly cold-sensitive. The broad, glossy, deep-green leaves carry the strong sweet, clove-and-anise flavor expected of a true Genovese basil, making it well suited for pesto and fresh culinary use. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes as they form to delay bolting and keep the plant bushy and productive through the season. Harvest leaves in the cool of the morning for the best flavor, taking no more than a third of the plant at a time.
